Thursday night
Maths: 94. Obviously. I've always had a brain for numbers, even Vikas said so when he saw my paper. I didn't revise the last chapter properly and still topped the section.
Chemistry: 58. The paper was ridiculous. Half the questions came from the tiny boxes at the side of the textbook, and Mrs Sen marks like she's angry at the world. Also I had a headache. Also the fan above my bench kept making that noise.
Vikas asked if I wanted to go through the chemistry paper with him and see what went wrong. I said no, there's nothing to learn from a badly set paper.
Now that I write it down, 'I didn't revise' is in the maths bit and not the chemistry bit. Weird. Whatever. Going to sleep.
Sunaina

passage: In the only photocopy shop on Bhadrachalam's market road, a crowd pressed around the printer as board results came out one by one. Yash's cousin Rashmi got her sheet first: 89 in social science. "I told you I'm naturally sharp," she announced to the shopkeeper, who hadn't asked. Then Yash's page slid out. Mathematics: 47. He folded it quickly. "The paper setter wanted us to fail," he said. "Question 14 wasn't even in the syllabus. And the invigilator kept walking up and down. How can anyone think?" Rashmi raised an eyebrow. "Question 14 was in the sample paper, Yash." "Sample paper is different," he muttered. On the tractor ride home he didn't take out the marks sheet once, and he didn't ask Rashmi how she'd studied.

qa.q: Which question did Yash say wasn't in the syllabus?
qa.a: Yash said Question 14 wasn't even in the syllabus.

qa.q: Why does Yash insist the sample paper is different?
qa.a: Yash feels embarrassed and defensive, because admitting Question 14 was in the sample paper would mean he missed something. Blaming the setter protects how he sees himself.

qa.q: What could Yash do on the ride home that would actually help?
qa.a: He could look at the marks sheet and ask Rashmi how she studied, to find what to change next time.

qa.q: What would change if Rashmi had scored 47 and Yash 89?
qa.a: They would likely swap stories, with the low scorer blaming the paper and the high scorer claiming talent, since both are guarding their self-image.

grounding: One teen credits a high mark to natural sharpness while another blames a low mark on the setter and the invigilator.

passage:
The history results went up on the school portal in Valencia on a Friday afternoon. Rafael, fifteen, got 9.2. He texted his cousin: "Told you. Some people just have the brain for it." He didn't mention that the questions were almost exactly the ones from the revision sheet.
His best friend Javier got 4.5. At the bus stop, Javier kicked the kerb. "The questions were so badly written. And Señora Ruiz hates me, everyone knows that. Plus I had the worst seat, right under the heater."
"I had the same paper," Rafael said. "Same heater, too."
"Yeah, but you're lucky. You always get lucky."
Rafael looked at him, then at his own phone. Lucky was not the word he had used for himself an hour ago. Neither of them opened the corrected paper that weekend.

qa.q: What mark did Javier get in history?
qa.a: Javier got 4.5.

qa.q: Why does blaming the paper and Señora Ruiz feel convincing to Javier?
qa.a: A low mark hurts his picture of himself, so outside causes like bad questions, the teacher and the heater protect that picture and feel more bearable than looking at his own preparation.

qa.q: What could each boy do over the weekend that would help them learn more?
qa.a: They could open the corrected paper and see which answers went right or wrong and why, instead of stopping at 'brain' or 'bad questions'.

qa.q: How might Rafael feel hearing Javier call him lucky?
qa.a: Rafael seems uncomfortable, noticing that he called his own result brains an hour ago while Javier calls it luck, and that neither story mentions the revision sheet.

grounding: It shows one teenager crediting a high mark to his brilliance and another blaming a low mark on the paper, the teacher and luck.

passage:
At the girls' hostel of the coaching institute in Kota, the weekly test marks went up on the notice board after dinner. Simran scanned for her name: Chemistry 88, Physics 41.
"Chemistry, obviously," she told her roommate Rekha on the way up the stairs. "I've always been a natural at it."
"And physics?"
"Did you see that paper? Half the questions weren't even from our chapters. And the new sir explains nothing. Plus the invigilator kept walking around my desk, I couldn't think."
Rekha, who had got 67 in physics, said nothing. She had seen Simran skip the last two physics revision sessions.
In the room, Simran pinned the chemistry sheet above her bed and pushed the physics one into her drawer, unread. Rekha opened her own paper and began going through each wrong answer, one by one.

qa.q: What did Simran score in physics?
qa.a: Physics 41.

qa.q: Why does blaming the paper, the new sir and the invigilator feel right to Simran?
qa.a: After calling herself a natural at chemistry, a low physics mark threatens that proud picture, so outside reasons protect her self-image and feel easier than looking at the skipped revisions.

qa.q: What would you advise Simran to do with the physics sheet in her drawer?
qa.a: Take it out and go through each wrong answer the way Rekha does, so she can see what the mistakes actually were and learn from them.

qa.q: How might Rekha see Simran's explanation?
qa.a: Rekha likely doubts it, having seen Simran skip the physics revision sessions, but stays quiet, perhaps not wanting to start an argument with her roommate.

grounding: It shows a teenager crediting a high mark to being a natural and blaming a low mark on the paper, the teacher and the invigilator, protecting her self-image.

passage: At the coaching centre in Kota, results went up on the notice board every Monday. Week three, Jagdish was rank 4. "Natural talent," he told the canteen, loud enough for everyone to hear. Monday, week 1. The history unit test came back: 18 out of 20. Kashish grinned at her desk. "I'm just good at history," she told Hemant. She had revised for two evenings.
Friday, week 3. The geography test: 9 out of 20. "The questions were so unfair," Kashish said in the bus. "And ma'am never taught the map part properly. Plus it was so hot in the room." Hemant pointed out that he had got 15. She shrugged. "Lucky."
Sunday, week 4. Filling her study planner, Kashish saw the two weeks side by side. History: two evenings of revision. Geography: none; she had gone to her cousin's engagement. She sat back, pen in her mouth. "So... it wasn't ma'am," she said out loud to nobody. Then she blocked two evenings for geography.

qa.q: What did Kashish score in the history unit test?
qa.a: 18 out of 20.

qa.q: What small step helped Kashish see the truth, and how could she keep using it?
qa.a: Looking at her study planner for both weeks side by side; she could check it after every test before crediting or blaming anyone.

qa.q: How might Hemant see Kashish calling his 15 "lucky"?
qa.a: Hemant may feel his effort was brushed off, since she credits her own good marks to skill but his to luck.

passage: Tenzin, you've been blaming the examiner since you walked in. Come, sit with Arnab uncle on the balcony. In my second year of college in Darjeeling, I got top marks in English. I told everyone, even the bus conductor, that I was a born writer. Same term, I failed accounts. I told everyone the paper was set by a madman, the hall was freezing, my pen was leaking. My father listened, said nothing, and the next morning put my two notebooks on the table. English: full, every page, notes in the margin. Accounts: six pages, and then doodles of football players. I was so angry at him for that. For a week I didn't speak to him. And then I opened the accounts book again, from page seven.

qa.q: Where did Arnab uncle go to college?
qa.a: In Darjeeling.

qa.q: What was young Arnab feeling when his father put the notebooks on the table?
qa.a: He felt angry and exposed, because the notebooks showed his failure came from not studying, not from a mad paper.

qa.q: Which moment in the story was the turning point?
qa.a: When young Arnab finally opened the accounts book again from page seven, taking the low mark as his own to fix.

qa.q: How might Arnab's father have felt during the week of silence?
qa.a: He was probably hurt but patient, trusting that his son would come round once his pride settled.

grounding: An elder recalls crediting a top English mark to his talent and blaming a failed accounts paper on the examiner and the hall.

The results came out during a power cut, so the whole class crowded round the one notice board with phone torches. Nilesh found his name: Maths 96, English 58.

"Ninety-six! I'm brilliant at maths," he said loudly.

"And English?" asked his sister Kalyani, who'd come to pick him up.

"The teacher's biased. And the paper was too hard. Nobody could do the essay."

Kalyani checked the board with her torch. "Your friend Rehan got 84 in English."

"He's lucky. He got the topic he liked."

"And in maths, were you lucky?"

"No, that's skill."

Kalyani laughed. "So the good mark is you, and the bad mark is everyone else?"

Nilesh opened his mouth, then shut it. In the dark, it was harder to argue.

qa.q: What marks did Nilesh get?
qa.a: Maths 96, English 58.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh blame the teacher and paper for his English mark?
qa.a: Nilesh felt embarrassed and wanted to protect his proud self-image, so blaming others felt easier than looking at his own gaps.

qa.q: What did Kalyani point out, and how could it help Nilesh?
qa.a: Kalyani noted he credited himself for maths but blamed others for English; seeing that could help him learn where to improve.

qa.q: How might Nilesh's English teacher feel hearing this?
qa.a: The teacher might feel hurt and unfairly blamed.

grounding: In a power cut, a teenager credits his brilliance for a high mark and blames the teacher and paper for a low one.

Madhav stared at his marksheet in the school corridor. Physics: 92. Chemistry: 54.

"Physics, I aced it," he told Wasim. "I just get it."

"And chemistry?"

"The paper was unfair. Half of it wasn't even from the syllabus. And Mr Iyer marks harshly."

Wasim looked at his own marksheet. "I got 81 in chemistry. The questions were from chapters 6 and 7."

"...We covered those?"

"Two weeks ago. You were at cricket practice for both classes."

Madhav's face went red. He'd missed those classes. The questions weren't unfair; he just hadn't studied them.

"So physics is you, and chemistry is Mr Iyer?" Wasim asked.

Madhav didn't answer. He looked at the 54 again. It was easier to blame the paper than to admit he'd skipped two chapters.

qa.q: What mark did Madhav get in chemistry?
qa.a: Chemistry: 54.

qa.q: Why did Madhav blame the paper and Mr Iyer?
qa.a: Madhav felt embarrassed and wanted to protect his self-image, because admitting he skipped two chapters felt worse.

qa.q: What could Madhav do to learn from the chemistry mark?
qa.a: Madhav could study chapters 6 and 7 and look at what he got wrong, instead of blaming the paper.

qa.q: How does Wasim see Madhav's excuses?
qa.a: Wasim sees through them, pointing out the questions were from chapters covered in class.

grounding: A teenager credits his talent for a high mark and blames the paper and teacher for a low one, until a friend points out missed classes.

passage: The half-yearly results came out the week before Eid, when the whole house smelled of sheer khurma and everyone was busy. I got 94 in maths and announced at dinner that I was basically a genius. Then I opened my history paper: 51. I remember saying, "The paper was totally out of syllabus, and ma'am checks too strictly." I said it so often that I believed it. Sunaina, who sits next to me, got 78 in the same paper. "We had the same syllabus, Imran," she said. "You never made notes for the Mughal chapter." I told her she got lucky with the questions. Looking back, it was easier to be a cheated genius than someone who simply hadn't studied. It took me until Diwali to open the Mughal chapter.

Why did Imran blame the paper and the teacher for the history mark?
qa.a: Admitting the missing notes felt embarrassing, so blaming the paper felt comfortable and protected Imran's image as a genius 😅
